}}The '''UEFA Women's European Championship''', also called the '''UEFA Women's EURO''', is the main competition in [[women's association football]] between national teams of the [[UEFA]] confederation. It is held every four years mostly in odd-numbered years, one year after the [[UEFA European Championship|men's]]. It was first held in 1984. The reigning champions are [[England women's national football team|England]], who won the tournament in 2022 and 2025. The most successful nation in the history of the tournament is [[Germany women's national football team|Germany]], with eight titles, followed by [[Norway women's national football team|Norway]] and England, each with two titles, and   [[Sweden women's national football team|Sweden]] and [[Netherlands women's national football team|Netherlands]] with one title each.
 
The latest edition of the UEFA Women's Championship was the 2025 tournament held in Switzerland after the previous edition was held in 2022 which was postponed from 2021 due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]. 

The next edition will be held in [[UEFA Women's Euro 2029|2029]] and it will be hosted by Germany.

==History==

===Previous European championships===

In 1957 in [[West Berlin]], a European Championship was staged by the International Ladies Football Association.<ref name="BPB07">{{cite web |title=Damenfußball in der Verbotszeit [Ladies' football in the banned era] |url=https://www.bpb.de/themen/sport/graue-spielzeit/65065/damenfussball-in-der-verbotszeit/ |website=BPB |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220218220314/https://www.bpb.de/themen/sport/graue-spielzeit/65065/damenfussball-in-der-verbotszeit/ |archive-date=18 February 2022 |date=4 September 2007}}</ref><ref name="Getty57">{{cite web |title=Women's european football championship scene from match germany (GFR) against England in Berlin (West-Berlin) . final result 0:4 05.Nov. 1957 |url=https://www.gettyimages.co.nz/detail/news-photo/sport-football-women-womens-european-football-championship-news-photo/548210661 |website=Getty Images |access-date=2022-07-24 |archive-date=2022-08-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220802100136/https://www.gettyimages.co.nz/detail/news-photo/sport-football-women-womens-european-football-championship-news-photo/548210661 |url-status=live }}</ref> Four teams, representing West Germany, the Netherlands, Austria, and the eventual winners, England, played the tournament at the [[Poststadion]],<ref name="BPB07"/><ref name="Getty57"/> at a time when women's football teams were officially forbidden by the [[German Football Association]], a ban that was widely defied.<ref name="TandF22">{{cite journal |title=A comparative analysis of the 1921 English Football Association ban on women's football in Britain and Ireland |journal=Sport in History |date=27 January 2022|volume=42 |issue=1 |pages=49–75 |doi=10.1080/17460263.2021.2025415 |last1=Skillen |first1=Fiona |last2=Byrne |first2=Helena |last3=Carrier |first3=John |last4=James |first4=Gary |s2cid=246409158 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Dfunk15">{{cite web |title=Frauenfußball-Verbot 1955 [Women's football ban 1955] |url=https://www.deutschlandfunk.de/frauenfussball-verbot-1955-die-weibliche-anmut-verschwindet-100.html |website=Deutschlandfunk |date=30 July 2015 |access-date=24 July 2022 |archive-date=5 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220805052706/https://www.deutschlandfunk.de/frauenfussball-verbot-1955-die-weibliche-anmut-verschwindet-100.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The Italian Women's Football Federation FICF, which eventually merged into the [[Italian Football Federation]], organised a [[1969 European Competition for Women's Football|European tournament in Italy in 1969]] for women's national teams, a tournament won by the home team, [[Italy women's national football team|Italy]], who beat [[Denmark women's national football team|Denmark]] 3–1 in the final.<ref name="1969rsssf">{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablese/eur-women69.html |title=Coppa Europa per Nazioni (Women) 1969 |publisher=Rsssf.com |date=19 March 2001 |access-date=12 September 2009 |archive-date=7 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221207181547/https://www.rsssf.org/tablese/eur-women69. |url-status=live }}</ref> The two nations were also the finalists of the [[1970 Women's World Cup]] in Italy.

Italy hosted another European women's tournament a decade later, the [[1979 European Competition for Women's Football]] – won by [[Denmark women's national football team|Denmark]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablese/eur-women79.html |title=Inofficial European Women Championship 1979 |publisher=Rsssf.com |date=15 October 2000 |access-date=12 September 2009 |archive-date=6 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221206013922/http://https/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

UEFA displayed little enthusiasm for women's football and were particularly hostile to Italy's independent women's football federation. [[Sue Lopez]], a member of England's squad, contended that a lack of female representation in UEFA was a contributory factor:<ref name="Lopez-WOTB">{{Cite book |last1=Lopez |first1=Sue |authorlink= Sue Lopez|title=Women on the Ball: A Guide to Women's Football |publisher=Scarlet Press |year=1997 |location=London, England |isbn=1857270169 |page=99}}</ref>

{{cquote|In 1971, UEFA had set up a committee for women's football, composed exclusively of male representatives, and by the time this committee folded in 1978 they had failed to organise any international competitions.<ref name="Lopez-WOTB"/>}}

===UEFA organised championships===

At a conference on 19 February 1980 UEFA resolved to launch its own competition for women's national teams.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.uefa.com/MultimediaFiles/Download/Women/General/01/99/05/49/1990549_DOWNLOAD.pdf |title=2013 Uefa Women's Competitions|publisher=[[UEFA]] |date=August 2013 |access-date=12 January 2014|page=4 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131217110606/https://www.uefa.com/MultimediaFiles/Download/Women/General/01/99/05/49/1990549_DOWNLOAD.pdf |archive-date=17 December 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref> The meeting minutes had registered the [[1979 European Competition for Women's Football|1979 competition]] as a "cause for concern".<ref name="Williams-ABG">{{cite book|title=A Beautiful Game: International Perspectives on Women's Football|last=Williams|first=Jean|authorlink=Jean Williams|publisher=[[Berg Publishers]]|year=2007 |isbn=978-1845206758 |page=30}}</ref> [[1984 European Competition for Women's Football qualification|Qualification]] for the first [[UEFA]]-run international tournament began in 1982, with the inaugural [[1984 European Competition for Women's Football|1984]] competition being won by [[Sweden women's national football team|Sweden]]. [[Norway women's national football team|Norway]] won the second competition in [[1987 European Competition for Women's Football|1987]]. A period of [[Germany women's national football team|German]] domination then followed, with Germany winning 8 of the 9 competitions from 1989 to 2013, interrupted only by [[Norway women's national football team|Norway]] in [[UEFA Women's Euro 1993|1993]]. [[Netherlands women's national football team|The Netherlands]] won in [[UEFA Women's Euro 2017|2017]] followed by [[England women's national football team|England]] winning the most recent two editions of the competition in [[UEFA Women's Euro 2022|2022]] and [[UEFA Women's Euro 2025|2025]].

From 1984 to 1995, the tournament was initially played as a four-team event. The 1997 edition was the first that was played with eight teams, followed by the 2001 and 2005 editions. The third expansion happened between 2009 and 2013 when 12 teams participated. From 2017 onwards 16 teams compete for the championship.<ref>{{cite web|title=Women's EURO and U17s expanded|url=https://www.uefa.com/news-media/news/0252-0ce27364ea6b-dda112b1c6f4-1000--women-s-euro-and-u17s-expanded/|publisher=UEFA|access-date=8 December 2011|date=8 December 2011|archive-date=17 September 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190917131736/https://www.uefa.com/womenseuro/news/newsid%3D1731832.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

The first three tournaments of the UEFA competition in the 1980s had the name "European Competition for Representative Women's Teams". With UEFA's increasing acceptance of women's football, this competition was given European Championship status by UEFA around 1990.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Leslie-Walker |first=Anika |last2=Schlenker |first2=Marisa |date=2020-07-08 |title=Four decades of UEFA Women's Championships "come home" |url=https://footballmakeshistory.eu/four-decades-of-uefa-womens-championships-come-home/ |access-date=2023-11-23 |website=Football Makes History |language=en-US |archive-date=2023-11-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231123194753/https://footballmakeshistory.eu/four-decades-of-uefa-womens-championships-come-home/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Only the [[UEFA Women's Euro 1991|1991]] and [[UEFA Women's Euro 1995|1995]] editions have been used as European qualifiers for a [[FIFA Women's World Cup]]; starting in 1999, women's national teams adopted the separate [[:Category:FIFA Women's World Cup qualification (UEFA)|World Cup qualifying competition and group system]] used in men's qualifiers.
